short: A small unit of ownership in a company, giving its holder a share of the company's profits and, usually, a vote on major decisions.
kid: Imagine your friend's lemonade stand is cut into 100 equal pieces. If you own one piece, a little part of the stand is yours, and so is a little part of the coins it earns.
detail: A stock, or equity share, represents fractional ownership of a company. Holders are entitled to a proportionate part of any profits paid out as dividends, a vote on matters such as electing directors, and a residual claim on assets if the company is wound up, after lenders and other creditors are paid. Their liability is limited to what they paid for the shares. Companies issue stock to raise capital without borrowing; investors then buy and sell it on exchanges such as NSE and BSE in India, where an individual stock is often called a scrip. Returns come from dividends and price changes, which reflect expectations of future profits. A common confusion is between face value and market price: a share with a face value of ₹10 may trade at ₹1,500, because face value is only an accounting figure.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 10 lakh shares outstanding and you buy 1,000 of them at ₹250 each, paying ₹2,50,000. You now own 0.1% of the company, so if it pays out a total dividend of ₹20 lakh, your share is ₹2,000.

short: A person or institution that owns at least one share of a company, and so owns part of that company.
kid: If you and three friends chip in to buy a lemonade stand, each of you owns a part of it. You all get a say in what it sells and some of the coins it makes.
detail: A shareholder owns one or more shares of a company and is therefore a part-owner. Equity shareholders typically have the right to vote at general meetings, receive dividends when declared, receive annual reports, and take part in rights and bonus issues in proportion to their holding. Their liability is limited to the amount invested, but they rank last in a liquidation, after lenders and creditors. In India, shareholders usually hold shares in demat form through a depository participant, and the register on the record date decides who receives each benefit. Groups include promoters, institutions such as mutual funds and FPIs, and retail investors. A common confusion is between shareholders and stakeholders: stakeholders also include employees, customers and lenders. Another is thinking a shareholder owns the company's assets directly; the company owns its assets, and shareholders own the company.
example: Say XYZ Ltd has 50 lakh shares and you hold 5,000 of them. You own 0.1% of the company, carry 5,000 votes on a poll at its AGM, and receive ₹20,000 if it declares a dividend of ₹4 per share.

short: The marketplace where shares of companies are first sold to investors and then bought and sold between investors, mainly on stock exchanges.
kid: Think of a busy fair where people trade cards of their favourite shops. When lots of people want a card, its price goes up; when few want it, the price goes down.
detail: The equity market is where ownership in companies changes hands. In the primary market, companies sell new shares to investors through IPOs, follow-on offers or rights issues, and the money goes to the company. In the secondary market, investors trade existing shares among themselves on exchanges; the company receives nothing directly, but this trading sets prices and gives investors an easy exit. India's main exchanges are NSE and BSE, regulated by SEBI, and trades there settle on a T+1 basis, the standard cycle since 2023 under the rules as of 2025. Prices respond to earnings, interest rates, liquidity and sentiment, so the market also acts as a running vote on corporate prospects and the wider economy. A common confusion is treating the market and an index as the same thing: the Nifty 50 or Sensex summarises only a slice of it.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells 1 crore new shares at ₹500 each in its IPO, raising ₹500 crore; that is the primary market. If you later buy 100 of those shares from another investor at ₹560, paying ₹56,000, that is the secondary market, and ABC receives none of that money.

short: The total stock-market value of a company, found by multiplying its share price by the number of shares outstanding.
kid: If a toy box holds 10 marbles and each marble could be swapped for 2 sweets, the whole box is worth 20 sweets. Working out that total for a whole shop is the idea here.
detail: Market capitalisation measures what the stock market values a company's equity at right now. It changes every time the share price moves, so it reflects expectations about future profits rather than the cost of the company's assets. It is used to rank and classify companies as large-, mid- or small-cap, to set weights in most stock indices, and to compare firms of different sizes. In India, the total market cap of all listed companies is often compared with GDP as a rough gauge of how richly the market is valued. A common confusion is treating market cap as the price of buying the whole business: an acquirer also takes on the debt and gets the cash, which is why enterprise value is used for that. Another is mixing up full market cap with free-float market cap, which counts only publicly tradable shares.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 50 crore shares outstanding and they trade at ₹800 each. Its market capitalisation is 50 crore × ₹800 = ₹40,000 crore. If the price falls 10% to ₹720, market cap drops to ₹36,000 crore.
formula: Market capitalisation = Share price × Total shares outstanding

short: Shares of the biggest listed companies by market value; in India, SEBI's rules as of 2025 count the top 100 by market capitalisation.
kid: Think of the biggest, oldest trees in the park. Everyone knows them, and they hardly sway when the wind blows, while small saplings bend a lot.
detail: A large-cap stock belongs to one of the most valuable listed companies. Under SEBI's mutual fund categorisation rules as of 2025, large caps are the 1st to 100th companies by full market capitalisation, and AMFI publishes the ranked list every six months. In the US the label usually means companies worth more than about $10 billion, though cut-offs vary by index provider. Large caps tend to be established businesses with diversified revenue, high liquidity, deep analyst coverage and lower volatility than smaller companies, and they dominate benchmarks such as the Nifty 50 and S&P 500. Under the same SEBI rules, large-cap mutual funds must keep at least 80% of their assets in these stocks. A common confusion is equating large with safe: big companies can still fall sharply, and size says nothing about whether the price is reasonable.
example: Say AMFI's list ranks ABC Ltd 85th by full market cap, so it counts as a large cap; if it slips to 120th at the next half-yearly review, it becomes a mid cap. Under the 2025 rules, a large-cap fund with ₹1,000 crore of assets must hold at least ₹800 crore in large caps.

short: Shares of medium-sized listed companies; in India, SEBI's rules as of 2025 count the 101st to 250th companies by market capitalisation.
kid: Think of children in middle school: bigger than the little ones but still growing fast. They grow quicker than grown-ups, and they stumble more often too.
detail: Mid caps sit between established large caps and riskier small caps. Under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025, they are the companies ranked 101st to 250th by full market capitalisation on AMFI's half-yearly list, and mid-cap mutual funds must keep at least 65% of their assets in them. In the US, mid caps are often described as companies worth roughly $2 billion to $10 billion. Many have proven business models but still have room to grow, so earnings can rise faster than at large caps, while price swings are typically larger and trading thinner. Indices such as the Nifty Midcap 150 and S&P MidCap 400 track the segment. A common confusion is assuming a mid cap stays one: categories shift as prices move, so today's mid cap can become tomorrow's large or small cap.
example: Say ABC Ltd ranks 180th by full market cap, so it is a mid cap. Under the 2025 rules, a mid-cap fund with ₹2,000 crore of assets must hold at least ₹1,300 crore in stocks ranked 101st to 250th, like ABC.

short: Shares of smaller listed companies; in India, SEBI's rules as of 2025 count every company ranked below the top 250 by market capitalisation.
kid: Small boats bob up and down a lot on the waves, while a giant ship barely moves. But small boats can also zip ahead quickly when the wind is good.
detail: Small caps are the less valuable listed companies in a market. Under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025, any company ranked 251st or lower by full market capitalisation is a small cap, and small-cap funds must keep at least 65% of their assets in them. In the US the term usually covers companies worth roughly $300 million to $2 billion, tracked by indices such as the Russell 2000. Small caps offer room for rapid growth and get less analyst coverage, so mispricing is more common, but they carry higher business risk, sharper price swings and thinner trading volumes, which can make them hard to sell in a panic. India's Nifty Smallcap 250 tracks the companies ranked 251st to 500th. A common confusion is equating a low share price with a small cap: size depends on market cap, not on the price of one share.
example: Say ABC Ltd's shares trade at ₹2,000 but it has only 1 crore shares, giving a market cap of ₹2,000 crore, which is small-cap territory. XYZ Ltd trades at just ₹40 but has 1,000 crore shares, so its market cap is ₹40,000 crore, twenty times ABC's.

short: Shares of very small listed companies, below even the usual small-cap range; in India, often those ranked beyond the top 500 by market value.
kid: Think of a tiny seedling in a pot. It might grow into a big tree, but a strong wind or one missed watering could also knock it over.
detail: Micro caps are the smallest listed companies. SEBI's categorisation rules do not define them separately, so in India the term usually refers to companies beyond the top 500 by full market cap; the Nifty Microcap 250 tracks those ranked 501st to 750th. In the US, micro caps are generally companies worth less than about $300 million. These stocks can deliver large gains when a small business scales up, but they come with thin trading, wide bid-ask spreads, limited disclosure and analyst coverage, and a higher risk of price manipulation; regulators in both countries have repeatedly warned about pump-and-dump schemes in tiny stocks. In India, many micro caps are placed under exchange surveillance frameworks such as the Additional Surveillance Measure (ASM). A common confusion is treating micro caps as cheap because their share price is low; size is about market cap, not price per share.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 2 crore shares trading at ₹150, a market cap of ₹300 crore, which puts it in micro-cap territory. If only 5,000 shares trade on an average day, that is just ₹7.5 lakh of turnover, so a buyer wanting ₹50 lakh of stock could push the price up sharply.

short: A share of a large, well-established, financially sound company with a long record of steady profits and, often, regular dividends.
kid: Think of the oldest, most trusted shop on your street. It has been open for years, everyone knows it, and it almost never lets people down.
detail: Blue-chip stocks belong to large, reputable companies known for durable businesses, strong balance sheets, consistent earnings and, often, a long dividend record. The term comes from poker, where blue chips traditionally carry the highest value. Blue chips usually appear in flagship indices such as the Nifty 50, Sensex and Dow Jones Industrial Average, are heavily owned by institutions, and are easy to trade in large amounts. Investors treat them as core holdings because they tend to fall less than smaller stocks in downturns. There is no official list or regulatory definition; it is a market label, not a category like SEBI's large-cap list. A common confusion is equating blue chip with risk-free: well-known giants can still decline for years or even fail, and buying a great company at too high a price can still give poor returns.
example: Say blue-chip ABC Ltd has paid a dividend every year for 25 years, and in a market crash its share price falls 15% while a small-cap index falls 30%. An investor with ₹1,00,000 in ABC would be down ₹15,000, against ₹30,000 for the same amount in the small-cap index.

short: A single number that tracks the combined price movement of a chosen group of shares, used to show how a market is doing.
kid: Instead of checking every child's marks, a teacher can look at the class average to see how the whole class did. This number is a class average for a basket of shops.
detail: A stock market index measures the performance of a basket of shares chosen to represent a market or segment. It starts at a base value on a base date, and later readings show how much the basket's value has changed since then. Most modern indices weight stocks by free-float market capitalisation, though some use price or equal weights. India's headline indices are NSE's Nifty 50 and BSE's Sensex; global examples include the S&P 500 and FTSE 100. Indices serve as benchmarks for fund performance, underlie index funds, ETFs and derivatives, and give a quick read on sentiment. A common confusion is thinking an index is itself a tradable asset: you cannot buy the Nifty directly, only funds or futures that track it. Another is forgetting that most headline indices exclude dividends.
example: Say an index starts at a base value of 1,000 when its constituents are worth ₹10 lakh crore in total. If their combined market value later rises to ₹13 lakh crore, the index reads 1,000 × 13 / 10 = 1,300, a 30% gain.
formula: Index value = (Current market value of constituents / Base market value) × Base index value

short: An index in which each company's influence is proportional to its market value, so bigger companies move the index more.
kid: When friends pull a rope together, the biggest friend pulls hardest and moves the rope the most. In this kind of basket, the biggest shops count the most.
detail: In a market-cap weighted index, each constituent's weight equals its market capitalisation divided by the total of all constituents. Most major indices, including the Nifty 50, Sensex, S&P 500 and MSCI indices, use free-float market cap, which counts only shares available to the public and leaves out promoter and other locked holdings; NSE applies this through an investible weight factor. The method mirrors the market's actual value, needs little trading to maintain because weights adjust automatically as prices move, and is easy for index funds to replicate. Its weakness is concentration: a handful of giants can dominate, and the stocks that have risen most gain the largest weights. A common confusion is assuming a company with a high total market cap must have a high index weight; a large promoter stake shrinks its free float and so its weight.
example: Say an index holds A, B and C with free-float market caps of ₹6,000 crore, ₹3,000 crore and ₹1,000 crore, giving weights of 60%, 30% and 10%. If A rises 10% and the others are unchanged, the index rises 6%, but a 10% rise in C alone lifts it only 1%.
formula: Weight of stock = Free-float market cap of stock / Sum of free-float market caps of all constituents

short: An index in which each stock's influence depends on its share price, so higher-priced shares move it more, regardless of company size.
kid: Imagine keeping score by adding up the price tags on three toys. The most expensive toy changes the total the most, even if it is a tiny toy.
detail: A price-weighted index adds up the share prices of its constituents and divides by a divisor. Each stock's weight is its price relative to the sum of prices, so a $300 share counts six times as much as a $50 share, whatever the companies' sizes. The divisor is adjusted after stock splits, constituent changes and some other corporate actions so the index does not jump for reasons unrelated to market moves. The best-known examples are the Dow Jones Industrial Average and Japan's Nikkei 225. The approach is simple and historic, dating from when indices were calculated by hand, but it is widely criticised because a share's price depends on how many shares exist, not on the company's value. A common confusion: a stock split lowers a company's price and so its influence on a price-weighted index, even though nothing about the business changed.
example: Say three stocks trade at $300, $150 and $50, and the divisor is 5, so the index is 500 / 5 = 100. A 10% rise in the $300 stock adds $30 and lifts the index to 106, while a 10% rise in the $50 stock adds $5 and lifts it only to 101.
formula: Index = Sum of constituent share prices / Divisor

short: An index that gives every company in it the same weight at each rebalance, so the smallest company counts as much as the largest.
kid: When you share sweets so every friend gets the same number, nobody gets more just for being bigger. This basket gives every shop the same share.
detail: An equal-weight index assigns each constituent an identical weight, for example 2% each in a 50-stock index, and resets the weights periodically, often every quarter, because price moves cause them to drift in between. Examples include the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index and the Nifty 50 Equal Weight index. Compared with a market-cap weighted index of the same stocks, it reduces concentration in the biggest names, tilts towards smaller companies, and at each rebalance sells recent winners and buys recent laggards. That has helped in some periods and hurt when a few mega caps led the market. It also brings higher turnover and trading costs for funds that track it. A common confusion is to think equal weight means equal risk: a volatile small stock at 2% still adds more risk than a stable giant at 2%.
example: Say ₹1,00,000 is split equally across four stocks at ₹25,000 each. If one stock rises 20% and the others are flat, the portfolio is worth ₹1,05,000, a 5% gain, and that stock's weight has drifted to about 28.6% until the next rebalance trims it back to 25%.
formula: Weight of each stock = 1 / Number of constituents (reset at each rebalance)

short: The periodic review in which an index provider adds or removes companies and resets weights so the index keeps following its rules.
kid: Every so often a team coach looks again at who is in the team. Some players join and some leave, so the team stays the best it can be.
detail: Index rebalancing is the scheduled update of an index's constituents and weights. Providers check eligibility rules such as free-float market cap, liquidity and listing history, then announce inclusions and exclusions a few weeks before an effective date. NSE Indices reviews the Nifty 50 twice a year, and MSCI reviews its indices every quarter. Rebalancing matters because trillions of dollars sit in index funds and ETFs that must buy additions and sell deletions around the effective date, often at the closing price, causing heavy volumes and sharp price moves. Active traders try to anticipate these flows. Weight changes, such as a revised free-float factor, can trigger flows even without any additions. A common confusion is to treat inclusion as a verdict on a company's quality: it is a mechanical outcome of the rules, and part of the price effect often reverses later.
example: Say passive funds tracking an index hold ₹50,000 crore in total, and a newly added stock gets a 0.5% weight. Those funds must buy about ₹250 crore of it around the effective date, which can be many times the stock's usual daily trading.

short: A stock market index of about 500 of the largest US listed companies, widely used as the main gauge of the US stock market.
kid: Picture a huge basket holding 500 of the biggest shops in America. Its score shows whether those shops, all together, are doing better or worse.
detail: The S&P 500, maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, tracks around 500 leading US companies and covers roughly 80% of the value of the US stock market. It took its 500-stock form in 1957. A committee chooses constituents using rules on size, liquidity, profitability and US domicile, and weights them by float-adjusted market capitalisation, so the largest technology companies carry heavy weight. It is the standard benchmark for US equity funds and underlies huge index funds, ETFs, futures and options. Indian investors can access it through international fund-of-funds and ETFs, subject to the overseas investment limits in force at the time. A common confusion is that it holds exactly 500 stocks: some companies have more than one share class listed, so the number of constituents is slightly above 500. Another is equating it with the Dow, a separate 30-stock, price-weighted index.
example: From its October 2007 closing high of 1,565 to its March 2009 low of 677, the S&P 500 fell about 57% during the global financial crisis. An investment of $10,000 that fell 57% to $4,300 then needed a gain of about 133% just to get back to $10,000.

short: An index tracking 30 large, well-known US companies by adding up their share prices; first published in 1896, it is among the oldest market gauges.
kid: Imagine keeping score by adding up the price tags of 30 famous toys. If the price tags go up, the score goes up. People have kept this score for more than a hundred years.
detail: The Dow Jones Industrial Average, usually called the Dow, was created by Charles Dow and first published in 1896 with 12 stocks; it expanded to 30 in 1928. It is now maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, and despite its name it includes companies from most sectors, not just industrials. It is price-weighted: the index equals the sum of the 30 share prices divided by the Dow divisor, which is adjusted for splits and constituent changes. As a result, a stock with a high share price moves the Dow more than a far larger company with a low price. Its long history and media fame make it a popular headline number, but most professionals prefer the broader S&P 500 as a benchmark. A common confusion is reading a large point move as dramatic: a 500-point fall is a far smaller percentage today than in 1987.
example: On 19 October 1987, Black Monday, the Dow fell 508 points, or 22.6%, its largest one-day percentage fall. Because it is price-weighted, if one constituent rises $10 and the divisor is, say, 0.2, the index rises 10 / 0.2 = 50 points from that stock alone.
formula: DJIA = Sum of the 30 constituent share prices / Dow divisor

short: An index covering nearly all companies listed on the US Nasdaq exchange, with bigger companies counting more; it is dominated by technology firms.
kid: Think of a long street where many shops sell gadgets and computers. This score adds up how all those shops are doing, and the biggest shops count the most.
detail: The Nasdaq Composite tracks almost all common stocks listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market, typically several thousand securities, including some non-US companies. It was launched in 1971 at a base value of 100 and is weighted by market capitalisation, so a few mega-cap technology and internet companies dominate its moves. That makes it a popular gauge of sentiment towards technology and growth stocks, and it tends to swing more than the S&P 500. The Nasdaq exchange itself, the first electronic stock market, lists companies from many sectors, not only tech. A common confusion is between the Composite and the Nasdaq-100: the Nasdaq-100 holds only the 100 largest non-financial Nasdaq companies and is the index behind popular ETFs. When a headline says the Nasdaq fell, it usually means the Composite.
example: The Nasdaq Composite closed at 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000, at the peak of the dot-com bubble, and fell to 1,114.11 by 9 October 2002, a drop of about 78%. It did not close above its 2000 peak again until April 2015.

short: An index of the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the US Nasdaq exchange, heavily weighted towards big technology firms.
kid: From a long street of shops, pick the 100 biggest gadget, toy and food shops. Their score together shows how the giants of that street are doing.
detail: The Nasdaq-100, launched in 1985, holds the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market, including some non-US firms. It uses a modified market-cap weighting: weights broadly follow company size, but rules cap the largest names to limit concentration. Membership is reviewed every December, with weights checked each quarter. Technology, communication services and consumer companies dominate it, so it is often used as a proxy for big tech. It underlies some of the world's most traded products, notably the Invesco QQQ ETF and Nasdaq-100 futures, and Indian investors can access it through international ETFs and fund-of-funds. A common confusion is to treat it as identical to the Nasdaq Composite: the Composite covers thousands of Nasdaq stocks, financials included, while the Nasdaq-100 excludes banks and other financial companies.
example: Say an Indian investor puts ₹1,00,000 into a Nasdaq-100 fund. If the index rises 10% in dollar terms and the dollar strengthens 3% against the rupee, the investment grows to about ₹1,00,000 × 1.10 × 1.03 = ₹1,13,300, a 13.3% rupee return before costs.

short: A US index of about 2,000 smaller companies, the most widely used benchmark for American small-company shares.
kid: Imagine 2,000 small corner shops across a big country. Watching how they all do together tells you whether the little shops are having a good or bad time.
detail: The Russell 2000, launched in 1984 and run by FTSE Russell, measures US small caps. The provider ranks US companies by total market capitalisation to build the Russell 3000; the largest 1,000 form the Russell 1000, and the next 2,000 form the Russell 2000. Constituents are then weighted by float-adjusted market cap. The index was historically reconstituted every June, an event that drives very large trading volumes; from 2026 FTSE Russell moved to twice-yearly reconstitution, in June and December. Because small companies depend more on domestic demand and bank borrowing, the Russell 2000 is closely watched as a gauge of the US economy and of sensitivity to interest rates. A common confusion is thinking it holds the 2,000 smallest listed US companies: it holds the 2,000 below the top 1,000, and truly tiny micro caps sit outside it.
example: Say a US company ranks 1,500th by market cap on rank day; it falls in the Russell 2000 because it sits between 1,001st and 3,000th. If it grows to rank 800th at a later reconstitution, it typically moves to the Russell 1000, and Russell 2000 index funds must sell it.

short: Any of the global stock indices built by MSCI, such as MSCI World and MSCI Emerging Markets, which guide trillions of dollars of international investment.
kid: Imagine a big world map with a basket of the best shops from each country. People far away look at these baskets to decide where to put their coins.
detail: MSCI, a US-based index provider, publishes thousands of equity indices. The best known are MSCI World, covering developed markets; MSCI Emerging Markets, covering developing economies including India; and MSCI ACWI, which combines both. Single-country indices such as MSCI India also exist. They use free-float adjusted market-cap weighting and are reviewed quarterly, with larger semi-annual reviews in May and November. Global pension funds, sovereign funds and ETFs benchmark to them, so changes in a country's or stock's weight trigger large passive flows; for India, an inclusion or a higher weight usually brings foreign portfolio inflows into the affected stocks. MSCI also classifies countries as developed, emerging or frontier, and a reclassification can reshape flows. A common confusion is thinking MSCI is an exchange or a regulator: it is a private company that designs indices and earns licensing fees.
example: Say a global fund of $10 billion tracks MSCI Emerging Markets, and India's weight in that index rises from 18% to 19% at a review. The fund must buy about $100 million of additional Indian stocks, since 1% of $10 billion is $100 million.

short: An index of the 100 largest companies listed on the London Stock Exchange, the main gauge of the UK stock market.
kid: Imagine picking the 100 biggest shops in Britain and putting them in one basket. The basket's score shows how those big British shops are doing.
detail: The FTSE 100, nicknamed the Footsie, tracks the 100 largest eligible UK-listed companies, weighted by free-float adjusted market capitalisation. It was launched on 3 January 1984 at a base of 1,000 and is run by FTSE Russell, part of the London Stock Exchange Group, with membership reviewed every quarter. The index is dominated by multinational sectors such as energy, mining, banking, consumer staples and pharmaceuticals, and most of its constituents' combined revenue is earned outside the UK. That is why a weaker pound often lifts the FTSE 100: overseas earnings are worth more when converted into sterling. A common confusion is treating it as a gauge of the British economy; the more domestically focused FTSE 250, covering the next 250 companies by size, is often a better barometer of UK conditions.
example: Say a FTSE 100 company earns $1 billion of profit abroad. If the pound falls from $1.25 to $1.20, those profits are worth about £833 million instead of £800 million in sterling, a rise of about 4% with no change in the business itself.

short: Japan's best-known stock index, tracking 225 large companies on the Tokyo Stock Exchange and weighted by share price rather than company size.
kid: Imagine a score made by adding up the price tags of 225 toys from Japan. The most expensive toys change the score the most.
detail: The Nikkei 225, published by the Nikkei newspaper group, tracks 225 leading companies listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange's Prime market. Like the Dow, it is price-weighted, so companies with high share prices, such as some retailers and chip-equipment makers, have outsized influence regardless of their market value; Nikkei applies adjustment factors to limit any single stock's weight. Constituents are reviewed twice a year. The index is famous for Japan's bubble: it peaked in December 1989 and then spent decades below that level, a lesson in how long an overvalued market can take to recover. Japan's other main benchmark, TOPIX, is market-cap weighted and covers far more companies, so the two can diverge. A common confusion is using the Nikkei and the Japanese market interchangeably; TOPIX is the broader gauge most institutions track.
example: The Nikkei 225 closed at a record 38,915.87 on 29 December 1989 and did not close above that level until 22 February 2024. An investor who bought an index fund at the 1989 peak waited more than 34 years just to get back to the same index level, ignoring dividends.

short: Hong Kong's main stock index, tracking the largest and most traded companies listed there, many of them mainland Chinese businesses.
kid: Picture a basket holding the biggest shops in the busy city of Hong Kong. Its score goes up when those shops do well and down when they struggle.
detail: The Hang Seng Index, launched in 1969 and compiled by Hang Seng Indexes Company, tracks the largest and most liquid companies listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong. It is weighted by free-float adjusted market capitalisation with a cap on any single stock, and it is reviewed quarterly. Over the past two decades mainland Chinese companies, from internet platforms to banks and insurers, have come to dominate it, so it is often read as a gauge of foreign investors' views on China. It is also sensitive to US interest rates, because the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar. A common confusion is between the Hang Seng Index and mainland indices such as the Shanghai Composite: mainland markets are dominated by local investors trading A-shares, while Hong Kong is an open market where global investors trade freely.
example: Say an investor holds a Hang Seng index fund worth $50,000. If the index falls 2% while the Hong Kong dollar stays within its peg band of 7.75 to 7.85 per US dollar, the holding loses about $1,000 in US-dollar terms.

short: Germany's leading stock index, tracking 40 major companies on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and, unusually, counting reinvested dividends in its value.
kid: Picture a basket of Germany's 40 biggest shops. When a shop hands out coins, the basket keeps them and puts them back in, so the score grows a little extra.
detail: The DAX tracks 40 of the largest and most liquid German companies listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, weighted by free-float market capitalisation with a cap on individual weights. It launched in 1988 with 30 members and expanded to 40 in September 2021, when a profitability test for new members was also added. Its constituents include global exporters in carmaking, chemicals, industrials and software, so it is sensitive to world trade and the euro. The DAX is unusual because its headline version is a performance index: dividends are treated as reinvested, while most headline indices, such as the Nifty 50 and S&P 500, track prices only. A common confusion is comparing DAX gains directly with price indices, which flatters the DAX by the amount of dividends; a price-only version of the DAX also exists for like-for-like comparison.
example: Say DAX constituents' share prices end a year unchanged but pay dividends worth 3% of their value. The performance DAX rises about 3% because those dividends are treated as reinvested, while a price-only index of the same 40 stocks would show 0%.

short: An index of 50 large, leading companies from countries that use the euro, the main benchmark for eurozone shares.
kid: Many countries in Europe use the same kind of coins. This score watches the 50 biggest shops from all those countries together.
detail: The Euro Stoxx 50, run by STOXX within the Deutsche Börse group, tracks 50 of the largest and most liquid companies from eurozone countries, weighted by free-float market capitalisation with a cap on individual weights. It launched in 1998, ahead of the euro's introduction, and its futures and options are among Europe's most traded equity derivatives. Because only eurozone countries qualify, it excludes major European companies based in the UK, Switzerland and the Nordic countries outside the euro. The broader STOXX Europe 600 covers 600 large, mid and small companies across Europe, including those non-euro markets, and is often the index meant when news refers to European stocks. A common confusion is treating the two as the same, or assuming Europe's biggest companies must be in the Euro Stoxx 50; Nestlé, for instance, is Swiss, so it is not.
example: Say an Indian investor puts €10,000 into a Euro Stoxx 50 fund when €1 costs ₹90, an outlay of ₹9,00,000. If the fund rises 5% to €10,500 but the euro falls 5% to ₹85.50, the holding is worth ₹8,97,750, a small rupee loss of ₹2,250 despite the gain in euros.

short: An index of the shares listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, the most quoted gauge of mainland China's stock market.
kid: Picture a huge basket holding almost every shop from one big Chinese city's market. Its score shows whether those shops, together, are doing well.
detail: The Shanghai Composite, officially the SSE Composite Index, tracks the shares traded on the Shanghai Stock Exchange. It was launched in 1991 with a base of 100 set in December 1990, and covers A-shares, priced in yuan, and B-shares, priced in foreign currency. It has traditionally weighted companies by total market value rather than free float, so large state-controlled banks and energy companies, which have relatively few freely traded shares, carry heavy weight. Mainland trading is dominated by domestic retail investors, which makes the market prone to sharp, policy-driven swings. Foreign investors reach A-shares mainly through the Stock Connect links with Hong Kong. A common confusion is treating it as the whole Chinese market: it excludes Shenzhen-listed companies and Chinese firms listed in Hong Kong or the US, so many professionals prefer the CSI 300, which spans Shanghai and Shenzhen.
example: Say a state-controlled bank has a total market value of 1,000 billion yuan but only 20% of its shares trade freely. A total-value weighting counts all 1,000 billion yuan, while a free-float index would count only 200 billion yuan, one-fifth as much.

short: South Korea's main stock index, tracking all common shares on the Korea Exchange's main board, weighted by company market value.
kid: Picture a basket with every big shop from South Korea inside. A few giant gadget shops are so big that they move the whole basket's score.
detail: KOSPI, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, covers all common stocks listed on the main KOSPI market of the Korea Exchange. It started at a base of 100 on 4 January 1980 and is weighted by market capitalisation. A few giants, led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, carry very large weights, so the index is closely tied to the global memory-chip cycle and to exports. Foreign investors account for a large part of trading, which makes the KOSPI a common barometer of appetite for emerging-market and Asian risk. The narrower KOSPI 200 underlies Korea's heavily traded futures and options. A common confusion is reading low Korean valuations as simple cheapness: the so-called Korea discount reflects long-standing governance concerns around family-run conglomerates, or chaebols, which recent reform drives aim to address.
example: Say one company makes up 20% of the KOSPI. If that stock falls 5% and every other constituent is flat, the index falls about 20% × 5% = 1% from that one stock alone.

short: A portion of a company's profits paid out to its shareholders, usually in cash, as a reward for owning its shares.
kid: Your lemonade stand earns some coins, and you and your friends own it together. When you split some of those coins among yourselves, each friend's handful is like this.
detail: A dividend is a distribution of a company's profits or accumulated reserves to its shareholders, usually in cash and in proportion to shares held. In India, the board can declare an interim dividend during the year, while a final dividend is recommended by the board and approved by shareholders at the AGM. Indian companies often announce dividends as a percentage of face value, so a 200% dividend on a ₹10 face-value share means ₹20 per share, not 200% of the market price. Dividends signal confidence in cash flows, but they are optional and can be cut. Under the rules as of 2025, Indian shareholders pay tax on dividends at their slab rates, with TDS above a threshold. A common confusion is thinking a dividend is free money: the share price typically drops by about the dividend amount on the ex-date.
example: Say ABC Ltd, with a face value of ₹10, declares a 150% dividend, which is ₹15 per share. If you hold 400 shares, you receive ₹6,000, and at a share price of ₹600 the dividend yield is ₹15 / ₹600 = 2.5%.
formula: Dividend per share = Total dividends paid / Number of shares outstanding

short: A one-time dividend paid outside a company's normal schedule, usually from an unusual windfall or surplus cash, and not expected to repeat.
kid: Your lemonade stand had a lucky day when a big party bought everything. You share the extra coins with your friends once, but you don't promise it will happen again.
detail: A special dividend is a non-recurring payout, separate from a company's regular interim or final dividends. Companies declare one after an exceptional cash event, such as selling a business or property, receiving a large settlement, or building up more cash than they can use productively. By labelling it special, management signals that investors should not expect it every year, which avoids raising the regular dividend to a level it may later have to cut. In India, several multinational subsidiaries and companies that sold divisions have paid large special dividends, and the record date and ex-date work as for any dividend. For stocks with futures and options, exchanges may adjust contracts for large dividends. A common confusion is treating a special dividend as a rise in ongoing income; analysts usually exclude it when calculating a stock's regular dividend yield.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells a division for ₹2,000 crore and pays a special dividend of ₹20 per share on its 50 crore shares, a total of ₹1,000 crore. An investor with 500 shares receives a one-off ₹10,000 on top of the regular final dividend of ₹5 per share, worth ₹2,500.

short: The date a company checks its register of shareholders to decide who will receive a dividend, bonus shares or another benefit.
kid: A teacher writes down who is in class on Friday, and only those children get a sticker. If you join the class on Monday, you missed the list.
detail: The record date is the cut-off on which a company, through its registrar and the depositories, identifies the shareholders entitled to a benefit such as a dividend, bonus issue, stock split or rights entitlement. Only investors recorded as owners at the end of that day qualify. Because trades take time to settle, buying on the record date itself is too late. Under the T+1 settlement cycle used in India since 2023 and in the US since May 2024, the ex-date and the record date generally fall on the same day, so you must buy by the previous trading day. Indian companies once used book closure, a period of several days when the share register was closed; listed companies now mostly announce a single record date. A common confusion is mixing up the record date with the payment date: the dividend is credited later.
example: Say ABC Ltd announces a ₹10 dividend with a record date on a Friday. Under T+1 the ex-date is that same Friday, so an investor who buys 200 shares on Thursday settles on Friday and receives ₹2,000, while one who buys on Friday gets nothing.

short: The first trading day on which buying a share no longer gets you its announced dividend or other benefit.
kid: A shop gives a free balloon to everyone already inside at noon. Anyone who walks in after noon can still shop, but gets no balloon.
detail: The ex-date is the day a stock starts trading without the entitlement to a declared dividend, bonus, split or rights issue; hence the labels ex-dividend, ex-bonus, ex-split and ex-rights. Anyone buying on or after the ex-date will not settle in time to be on the register on the record date. With T+1 settlement in India since 2023 and in the US since May 2024, the ex-date and record date are generally the same day. On the ex-date, the share price usually opens lower by roughly the value of the benefit, since new buyers no longer get it; for bonuses and splits, exchanges and charting tools adjust past prices so the drop does not look like a crash. A common confusion is believing you can buy just before the ex-date, collect the dividend and sell at the same price: the price drop and taxes usually remove any easy gain.
example: Say ABC Ltd closes at ₹500 the day before its ex-dividend date and pays a ₹10 dividend. All else equal, it may open near ₹490 on the ex-date: a holder of 100 shares sees the holding fall from ₹50,000 to ₹49,000 but is owed ₹1,000 in dividend, so total wealth is unchanged before tax.
formula: Expected ex-dividend price ≈ Previous closing price - Dividend per share

short: Any event started by a company that changes its shares or what shareholders receive, such as dividends, bonus issues, splits, rights issues or mergers.
kid: Sometimes the owner of a sweet shop decides to change things, like giving everyone extra sweets or cutting big chocolate bars into smaller pieces. Each of those decisions is one of these.
detail: A corporate action is a decision by a company's board, often needing shareholder approval, that affects its securities or their holders. Mandatory actions apply automatically to everyone, such as cash dividends, bonus issues, stock splits and mergers. Voluntary actions require each holder to choose, such as subscribing to a rights issue or tendering shares in a buyback or open offer. In India, listed companies must disclose these to the exchanges under SEBI's listing regulations and fix a record date, and the depositories credit benefits to demat accounts. Exchanges adjust historical prices, index divisors and derivative contracts so comparisons stay fair. Investors need to track them because they change the number of shares, the price, the cash received or the tax position. A common confusion is treating every corporate action as value-creating: splits and bonuses change only the slicing, not the size of the pie.
example: Say ABC Ltd announces a 1:1 bonus. An investor with 200 shares at ₹1,000 ends up with 400 shares near ₹500, still worth ₹2,00,000, and the exchange adjusts past prices on charts so the ex-date does not look like a 50% crash.

short: Free extra shares a company gives existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, made by turning saved-up profits into share capital.
kid: A fair gives everyone one extra ticket for every ticket they already hold, but now each ticket buys only half as many rides. You have more tickets, but the same fun.
detail: In a bonus issue, a company capitalises part of its free reserves or securities premium and issues new fully paid shares to existing holders at no cost, in a fixed ratio; in India a 1:2 bonus means one new share for every two held. Face value per share stays the same, share capital rises and reserves fall by the same amount, so total equity, the company's value and each holder's percentage ownership are unchanged. The share price adjusts down on the ex-bonus date. Companies use bonuses to make shares more affordable, improve liquidity and signal confidence. Under SEBI's issue rules as of 2025, a bonus cannot be paid out of revaluation reserves. A common confusion is seeing bonus shares as extra wealth: the pie is the same size, cut into more slices. A split differs because it lowers face value instead.
example: Say you hold 100 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹900, worth ₹90,000, and it announces a 1:1 bonus. You receive 100 more shares and the price adjusts to about ₹450, so your 200 shares are still worth about ₹90,000.
formula: Ex-bonus price ≈ Cum-bonus price × A / (A + B), for a bonus of B new shares for every A held

short: Dividing each existing share into several smaller shares with a lower face value, so holders own more shares at a proportionally lower price.
kid: If you break a chocolate bar into smaller squares, you have more pieces, but it is still the same bar. Nothing extra to eat appeared.
detail: A stock split, or sub-division, divides each existing share into several shares by reducing face value; a split from ₹10 face value to ₹2 creates five shares for each one held. Share capital, reserves and every shareholder's percentage ownership stay the same, and the market price adjusts in proportion on the ex-split date. Companies split when the price has risen high enough to deter small investors or reduce trading liquidity; a lower price per share can make buying easier and widen the shareholder base. In the US, where par values are nominal, splits are usually quoted as 2-for-1 or 4-for-1. A common confusion is treating a split as a bonus issue: a bonus keeps face value and converts reserves into share capital, while a split leaves reserves untouched and lowers face value. Neither creates value by itself.
example: Say you own 100 shares of ABC Ltd with a face value of ₹10, trading at ₹2,500, worth ₹2,50,000. After a split to ₹2 face value, you hold 500 shares trading near ₹500, still worth ₹2,50,000.
formula: Split ratio = Old face value / New face value; Post-split price ≈ Pre-split price / Split ratio

short: Combining several existing shares into one share with a higher face value, so holders own fewer shares at a proportionally higher price.
kid: If you trade ten small coins for one big coin worth the same, you have fewer coins but can still buy exactly the same toys.
detail: A reverse stock split, or consolidation, merges a fixed number of existing shares into one, raising the face value and the price per share in the same proportion; a 1-for-10 consolidation of ₹1 shares produces one ₹10 share for every ten held. Ownership percentages and company value are unchanged at the moment it happens. Companies usually consolidate when the share price has fallen very low, to shed a penny-stock image, attract institutional investors or meet exchange rules; US exchanges such as Nasdaq and the NYSE, for example, require a minimum share price of $1 for continued listing. Fractional entitlements are typically settled in cash. A common confusion is reading a reverse split as good news: it often follows past distress, and many such stocks keep falling afterwards. The share count drops, but the business is unchanged.
example: Say you own 1,000 shares of ABC Ltd with a face value of ₹1, trading at ₹3, worth ₹3,000. After a 1-for-10 consolidation, in which every ten shares become one, you hold 100 shares of ₹10 face value trading near ₹30, still worth ₹3,000.
formula: Post-consolidation price ≈ Pre-consolidation price × Number of old shares combined into one new share

short: An offer letting existing shareholders buy new shares, usually at a discount, in proportion to what they already own.
kid: A club lets its current members buy new badges first, at a lower price. Members who skip the offer end up owning a smaller part of the club.
detail: A rights issue lets a listed company raise fresh equity from its existing shareholders, who can subscribe to new shares in a fixed ratio, such as 1 for every 5 held, at a price usually below the market. It is a way to fund growth or repair a balance sheet without bringing in new owners. Shareholders who subscribe keep their percentage stake; those who do nothing are diluted. In India, rights entitlements are credited to demat accounts and can be traded on the exchange or renounced to others for a limited window, so non-subscribers can capture some value. On the ex-rights date, the share price tends to adjust towards the theoretical ex-rights price. A common confusion is seeing the discount as a free gain: it is offset by the fall in the share price, so simply ignoring the offer costs money.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at ₹200 and offers 1 new share for every 5 held at ₹140. Five shares worth ₹1,000 plus one new share at ₹140 make six shares worth ₹1,140, so the theoretical ex-rights price is ₹1,140 / 6 = ₹190.
formula: TERP = (N × Market price + n × Subscription price) / (N + n), where n new shares are offered for every N held

short: Shares for which investors have paid only part of the issue price so far, with the rest due later when the company calls for it.
kid: You pick a bicycle at the shop and pay some coins now, promising the rest later. You can ride it, but you must bring the rest of the coins when the shop asks.
detail: Partly paid-up shares are issued with only part of the price collected upfront; the balance is collected through one or more calls, such as a first call and a final call, on dates the board sets. Until fully paid, they trade on exchanges under a separate symbol and usually carry dividends and voting rights in proportion to the amount paid up. If a holder fails to pay a call, the company can forfeit the shares after due notice. Companies use the structure, most often in rights issues, to make large fund-raisings easier for shareholders by spreading payments. A well-known Indian example is Reliance Industries' roughly ₹53,000 crore rights issue in 2020, which was issued partly paid. A common confusion is valuing partly paid shares like fully paid ones: their price should roughly equal the fully paid price minus the amount still owed.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues rights shares at ₹400, payable ₹100 on application, ₹150 on first call and ₹150 on final call. If the fully paid shares trade at ₹520, the partly paid shares, with ₹300 still owed, should trade near ₹520 - ₹300 = ₹220.
formula: Fair price of partly paid share ≈ Fully paid share price - Amount still to be paid

short: Company-issued rights to buy new shares from that company at a fixed price within a set period, with no obligation to do so.
kid: A shop gives you a special ticket that lets you buy a toy later for today's price. If the toy gets pricier, the ticket is great; if it gets cheaper, you just don't use it.
detail: A warrant is a long-dated right, issued by a company, to subscribe to its new shares at a preset exercise price before expiry. When holders exercise, the company issues fresh shares and receives cash, so existing shareholders are diluted. This differs from an exchange-traded call option, which is written by another investor and settled without any new shares being created. In India, warrants are most often issued on a preferential basis, frequently to promoters, to raise money in stages. Under SEBI's rules as of 2025, at least 25% of the price must be paid upfront and conversion must happen within 18 months, failing which the upfront amount is forfeited. In some markets, warrants are attached to bonds or IPO units to make the deal more attractive. A common confusion is ignoring dilution: analysts count in-the-money warrants when calculating diluted EPS.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues warrants, each convertible into one share at ₹200 within 18 months, with ₹50 paid upfront and ₹150 due on conversion. If the share trades at ₹320 at conversion time, the holder pays ₹150 more for a share worth ₹320, a gain of ₹320 - ₹200 = ₹120 per warrant on the total ₹200 paid.
formula: Intrinsic value of a warrant = max(0, Share price - Exercise price) × Shares per warrant

short: The portion of a company's shares that is readily available for public trading, excluding stakes held by controlling owners, governments and other locked-in holders.
kid: A family owns a big jar of marbles. Mum keeps most of them on a high shelf, and only the marbles in the small bowl can be swapped with friends.
detail: Free float is the part of a company's equity that ordinary investors can actually buy and sell. It excludes holdings of promoters and promoter groups, strategic and government stakes, cross-holdings and shares under lock-in. Index providers multiply full market cap by a free-float factor, which NSE calls the investible weight factor, to get free-float market cap, which then sets index weights. A low free float means fewer shares change hands, which can make prices more volatile and limit how much large funds can buy. In India, listed companies must meet a minimum public shareholding, 25% under the rules as of 2025, with extra time allowed for very large IPOs and some public sector companies. A common confusion is equating free float with public shareholding: some non-promoter holdings, such as locked-in pre-IPO stakes or strategic investments, are excluded from free float too.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 100 crore shares trading at ₹500, a full market cap of ₹50,000 crore, and promoters hold 60%. Its free-float factor is 0.40, so its free-float market cap is ₹20,000 crore, and that is the figure an index such as the Nifty 50 uses to set its weight.
formula: Free-float market cap = Share price × Shares outstanding × Free-float factor
